items.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to its Jev model in the week before this post's date (2026-09-25).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's 'SystemOne' model (the product/API is called SystemOne).
The TypeSafe Jev documentation exists at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
TypeSafe's Jev provides AI primitives that let applications, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev comes with a 'powerful' set of AI primitives.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi makes the gap between designing ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanish.
AI agents can now build and manage infrastructure, handling provisioning and day-to-day scaling and reliability decisions while humans define how the infrastructure should work.

The GeoDeploy repository exists at https://github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
GeoDeploy (pulumi/devx-geodeploy) is released as open source and is available today.
Unlike a general-purpose LLM (which returns free text), Jev does not return free text but typed answers with calibrated confidence.
Jev returns typed answers together with calibrated confidence scores.
Jev exposes three decision primitives: choice() (multiple choice), score() (confidence-scored rating against a rubric), and noul() (yes/no).
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick along with a confidence value.
Jev's choice() primitive returns a probability distribution across all supplied options.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a caller-described rubric of levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question and returns a single probability.
Jev's choice() cannot return an answer that is not one of the options supplied (a closed-list selection cannot hallucinate an out-of-list value by construction).
A single Jev SystemOne call accepts a state object plus a set of multiple questions (choice/score/noul) and answers them all in one call.
TypeSafe's SDK is published as the npm package `@typesafe-ai/sdk` and exports `choice`, `noul`, and `score`.

The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` exposes a `TypeSafeClient` class with a `systemOne({ state, questions })` method whose result has an `answers` object keyed by question, with fields such as `.choice`, `.confidence`, `.noul`, and `.score`.
TypeSafe's guidance for writing score rubrics advises to "describe situations, not degrees."
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric.
In practice CPU utilization is usually paired with other autoscaling signals such as median end-to-end request latency or error rates.
